newsitem.title: CONGO: Brazzaville firing traps French ambassador.
newsitem.headline: Brazzaville firing traps French ambassador.

text.p: France's ambassador to Congo, the only foreign emissary left in battle-torn Brazzaville, got stuck in his embassy on Tuesday as a fresh shooting match erupted outside.

Ambassador Raymond Cesaire, whose 30 gendarmes are the only foreign force in the city, had earlier done the rounds of the fighting parties and other key figures as he pressed on with so far fruitless efforts to restore a proper peace.
One mortar shell landed about 100 metres (yards) from the embassy in the disputed heart of the capital beside the Congo river before the fighting subsided and calm returned.
For almost a week a "ceasefire" has held -- though to anyone not witness to the relentless bombardments that preceded it, the truce seemed more like a war.

Shelling and small-arms fire have been part of the daily diet for nerve-torn citizens, with a 90-minute artillery duel on Monday providing the worst, but not the last, breach of the ceasefire that both sides agreed to observe until the weekend.

Estimates put the dead at 1,000 to 3,000 after the 12 days of battles in early June that erupted when President Pascal Lissouba tried to disarm the militia of his adversary, the former one-party ruler Denis Sassou Nguesso.
U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun is trying to dispatch an African intervention force as soon as possible to the city that faces Kinshasa, capital of the former Belgian Congo, across the river.

"The most urgent and important thing is to induce the protagonists to stop fighting, to cease fire and also to commit themselves to negotiations to find a solution to this problem," Sahnoun told Radio France International.
Togo and Senegal on Monday became the first countries to offer troops for the force of around 1,700 soldiers.

Lissouba's presidency -- which some analysts say is in the weaker military position -- welcomed the force but insisted it should not simply solidify the frontlines that criss-cross the heart of the former capital of French Equatorial Africa.
"It must be a force which will confiscate weapons, particularly heavy ones, and not a force which will cut the town in two," one presidency source told Reuters.

Lissouba blames Sassou's "Cobras" for Monday's fighting, saying they shelled parliament to stop the swearing in of a Constitutional Council that has the power to grant the president an extension to his term by up to 80 days.

Presidential elections were due to have taken place at the end of July. The fighting has made that date unrealistic but all outside mediators have said rescheduling them must form part of any agreement.
Sassou, Lissouba and city mayor Bernard Kolelas, whose own militia has remained neutral in the latest war, were all front runners.
In the end, the Council was sworn in on Monday at an alternative venue, the Palace of Friendship, but has not yet ruled on Lissouba's mandate, the presidency source said.
Kolelas, Brazzaville's mayor, was due to continue his own mediation on Tuesday by assembling Congolese politicians in Bacongo, a southern suburb he controls.
His efforts nearly ran aground on Monday when two shells slammed into Bacongo, wounding six people.

The artillery duel also risked dragging ex-Zaire towards the conflict when seven shells landed near Kinshasa. The angry government said it had been deliberately targeted by one of the warring sides and would defend itself if it happened again.
